newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Prodi throws down budget gauntlet.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Prodi throws down budget gauntlet.

text.p: Italy's cabinet has called a meeting for Friday to approve the 1997 budget, signalling the government may be ready to defy hard left allies to try to railroad Italy into a planned single European currency.

The announcement came only hours before Prime Minister Romano Prodi was due to meet party allies on Thursday in a last-ditch effort to convince the Communist Refoundation party to accept cuts in pensions and health spending in the budget.

The summit of leaders of parties in the centre-left government and Refoundation chief Fausto Bertinotti had been due to take place on Wednesday but was put back for 24 hours while a flurry of behind-the-scenes talks continued.
The government relies on support from Bertinotti's party in the lower house of parliament
Prodi's efforts to put together a stringent budget that would keep alive Italy's hopes of joining a European currency union by the starting date of 1999 have gained increasing urgency in recent days.

The Milan daily Corriere della Sera said the government was now preparing a budget of around 38.5 trillion lire ($25.3 billion) in spending cuts and increased revenues, well above an originally planned package of 32.4 trillion lire.
This would be followed in coming months by an extraordinary "tax for Europe" which would raise a further 22 trillion lire through a once-off increase in income tax, the newspaper said.

The planned extraordinary tax is likely to receive a hostile reception in a country which already bears one of the heaviest tax burdens in Europe. A Datamedia opinion poll conducted on Wednesday showed 56.4 percent of a sample of 1,002 Italians were not prepared to pay the "European super tax".

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, widely seen as the standard-bearer of budgetary rigour, was quoted as saying that Italy's deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio had to fall to three percent by the end of 1997.

The target is one of the key guidelines laid out in the Maastricht treaty, which mapped out the path towards European economic and monetary union (EMU). Ciampi said the initial 1997 budget would take the deficit-GDP ratio to only 4.5 percent.
"With the second phase we must reach the three percent as called for by Maastricht," Ciampi said.

He is calling for a "solidarity" tax on pensions which would hit hardest at so-called "baby pensioners" -- people who are able to draw benefits before reaching statutory retirement age. Increased healthcare charges are also on the cards.
Armando Cossutta, Bertinotti's number two in Communist Refoundation, was in uncomprising mood as the summit meeting with Prodi drew near.
"We have been repeating both to Prodi and to Ciampi for several days now that we cannot accept even minimum cuts to pensions," Cossutta told Corriere della Sera.
A prominent industrialist urged the government to ignore the hard-left's objections and appeal to the right-wing opposition to help vote the budget through parliament.

"He (Prodi) should appeal to the sense of responsibility of the opposition. We are not interested in what kind of (parliamentary) majority approves the budget," said Giorgio Fossa, chairman of the industrial employers' confederation.
Newspaper commentators were critical of Bertinotti's all-out support for Italy's army of pensioners, saying they should also pay their share of the cost of joining a currency union.
